params.question: During a post-mortem examination of the scalp, what finding most reliably distinguishes a laceration from an incised wound?

answers.text: Irregular and ragged wound margins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Irregular margins are seen in lacerations, but a clean blunt object such as a hammer face can produce deceptively straight margins that mimic an incised wound. Tissue bridges are the more reliable sign.

answers.text: Presence of tissue bridges crossing the wound bed

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tissue bridges — thin strands of intact tissue spanning the wound — form because blunt force tears tissue unevenly, leaving some strands intact. A sharp weapon cuts cleanly through all layers, so tissue bridges are never found in incised wounds.

answers.text: The amount of subcutaneous haemorrhage surrounding the wound

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Subcutaneous haemorrhage can accompany both lacerations and incised wounds depending on the vascularity of the area and force applied. It does not reliably distinguish the two.

answers.text: Depth of penetration through all scalp layers

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Wound depth depends on the force applied and the instrument used, not on whether the mechanism was blunt or sharp. Both lacerations and incised wounds can penetrate to the same depth.

overallFeedback.feedback: The most reliable distinguishing feature is tissue bridges — thin strands of intact tissue crossing the wound bed. These form only with blunt-force tearing and are always absent in sharp-force incised wounds, even when other features like margin shape are ambiguous.

Correct. Tissue bridges are the hallmark of a laceration — they form because blunt force tears tissue unevenly, leaving strands intact. A sharp weapon cuts through all layers cleanly, so tissue bridges are always absent in incised wounds.

params.question: A stab wound to the neck has torn the internal jugular vein at a point above the level of the heart. How does this injury cause fatal venous air embolism?

answers.text: Blood loss from the torn vein floods the lungs, causing secondary drowning

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Haemorrhage from a jugular vein causes hypovolaemic shock, not pulmonary flooding. Venous air embolism is a distinct mechanism where air, not blood, obstructs the pulmonary circulation.

answers.text: Negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration draws air into the open vein, which blocks pulmonary circulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When a jugular vein tear lies above heart level, the negative pressure generated during each inspiration sucks air into the venous system. Air collects in the right heart and pulmonary vessels, forming an air lock that fatally blocks circulation.

answers.text: Air trapped in the cervical soft tissues compresses the trachea, causing mechanical asphyxia

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Surgical emphysema (air in neck tissues) is a different pathology. In venous air embolism, air enters the bloodstream directly through the torn vein, not the surrounding tissues.

answers.text: Blood clots from the tear site embolise to the pulmonary arteries

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pulmonary thromboembolism is a separate mechanism involving blood clots. In venous air embolism, the fatal obstruction is caused by air bubbles drawn into the venous system, not by thrombi.

overallFeedback.feedback: In venous air embolism, a torn jugular vein positioned above heart level allows air to be sucked in during inspiration by negative intrathoracic pressure. The air travels to the right heart and blocks pulmonary circulation — a distinct mechanism from haemorrhage, thromboembolism, or tissue emphysema.

Correct. When a torn jugular vein lies above heart level, negative intrathoracic pressure during inspiration draws air into the vein. The air travels to the right heart and pulmonary vessels, creating a fatal air lock that obstructs circulation.

interactions.label: A 22-year-old woman jumps feet-first from the third floor of a burning building

params.question: A 22-year-old woman jumps feet-first from the third floor of a burning building and lands on concrete. Which combination of injuries constitutes the classic triad for this landing position?

answers.text: Skull vault fracture, cervical spine dislocation, and bilateral femur fractures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This pattern suggests a head-first landing where force concentrates on the skull and cervical spine immediately. In a feet-first landing, the head and cervical spine are among the last structures to receive force.

answers.text: Bilateral calcaneal fractures, lumbar compression fractures, and wrist fractures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In a feet-first landing, force transmits upward sequentially: the calcaneus absorbs the initial impact, the lumbar spine compresses under axial load, and the outstretched hands sustain wrist (Colles') fractures as the body pitches forward.

answers.text: Bilateral ankle fractures, pelvic ring disruption, and thoracic burst fractures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While high-energy falls can produce many skeletal injuries, the specific classic triad described in forensic medicine for feet-first falls is calcaneal, lumbar, and wrist fractures — reflecting sequential force transmission from the point of first contact.

answers.text: Bilateral tibial plateau fractures, sacroiliac joint disruption, and cervical compression fractures

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The calcaneus, not the tibial plateau, is the first weight-bearing structure to absorb impact in a feet-first landing. The classic triad traces force from calcaneus through lumbar spine to outstretched wrists.

overallFeedback.feedback: In a feet-first landing, force travels upward in sequence: calcaneus → lumbar spine → wrists (from outstretched hands bracing the fall). This classic triad — bilateral calcaneal fractures, lumbar compression fractures, and wrist fractures — is key to forensic reconstruction of fall circumstances.

Correct. The classic triad of a feet-first fall — bilateral calcaneal fractures, lumbar compression fractures, and wrist fractures — reflects sequential upward transmission of force from the point of first impact through the axial skeleton.

interactions.label: An earthquake victim trapped under rubble for eight hours is conscious and talki

params.question: An earthquake victim trapped under rubble for eight hours is conscious and talking while pinned, but collapses and dies within minutes of being freed. What is the most likely immediate cause of death?

answers.text: Massive haemorrhage from previously compressed blood vessels once the pressure is released

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While haemorrhage can occur after release, the classic sudden death at rescue in crush syndrome results from a metabolic cause — hyperkalaemia — not from vascular bleeding. The compression may actually have been tamponading any torn vessels.

answers.text: Fat embolism from crushed long bone marrow entering the bloodstream

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Fat embolism syndrome typically manifests 24–72 hours after long bone fractures, not within minutes of release. The acute death in crush syndrome is from a different mechanism entirely.

answers.text: Sudden cardiac arrhythmia from a surge of potassium released by damaged muscle cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: When crushed muscle cells release their contents upon decompression, the potassium surge disrupts cardiac conduction, causing ventricular fibrillation within minutes. This is why crush syndrome victims can die at the very moment of rescue despite appearing stable while trapped.

answers.text: Acute renal failure from myoglobin blocking the kidney tubules

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Myoglobinuric renal failure is a real and serious complication of crush syndrome, but it develops over hours to days as myoglobin precipitates in the renal tubules. It cannot account for death occurring within minutes of rescue.

overallFeedback.feedback: In crush syndrome, sudden death at the moment of rescue is caused by hyperkalaemia. Damaged muscle cells dump potassium into the bloodstream upon decompression, triggering fatal ventricular arrhythmias within minutes — distinct from renal failure, which develops over hours to days.

Correct. Sudden death at rescue in crush syndrome results from hyperkalaemia — damaged muscle cells release potassium upon decompression, triggering fatal cardiac arrhythmias within minutes. Renal failure from myoglobin is a later complication, not the immediate cause.

interactions.label: A forensic pathologist is asked to identify the type of intracranial haemorrhage

params.question: A forensic pathologist is asked to identify the type of intracranial haemorrhage at post-mortem. Which set of features correctly identifies an epidural haematoma?

answers.text: Crescent-shaped collection crossing suture lines, caused by torn bridging veins

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes a subdural haematoma. Blood from torn bridging veins collects between dura and arachnoid in a crescent shape, and because it lies beneath the dura, it crosses suture lines freely.

answers.text: Blood filling the basal cisterns and cortical sulci, from ruptured cortical vessels or aneurysm

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes a subarachnoid haemorrhage. Blood in the cerebrospinal fluid spaces is a completely different compartment from the epidural space.

answers.text: Biconvex (lens-shaped) collection that does not cross suture lines, from rupture of the middle meningeal artery

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An epidural haematoma is biconvex because blood collects between the skull and dura, which is tightly adherent at suture lines and limits the spread. It arises from the middle meningeal artery at the fracture site and classically presents with a lucid interval.

answers.text: Haemorrhage within the brain parenchyma at the contre-coup site, from shearing of small intracerebral vessels

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This describes an intracerebral haemorrhage. Epidural haematomas are extradural — they collect entirely outside the brain substance, between the skull bone and the dura mater.

overallFeedback.feedback: An epidural haematoma is lens-shaped (biconvex) and does not cross suture lines, because the dura is firmly attached to the skull at these points. It results from middle meningeal artery rupture and classically shows a lucid interval — distinguishing it from the crescent-shaped subdural haematoma caused by torn bridging veins.

Correct. The epidural haematoma is biconvex because the dura's attachment at suture lines confines the blood collection. It results from middle meningeal artery rupture at a fracture site and classically shows a lucid interval before rapid neurological deterioration.
